content: 1. Sodium thiosulfate is an FDA-approved antidote used in conjunction with sodium nitrite for the treatment of acute, life-threatening cyanide poisoning. 2. Common adverse reactions to sodium thiosulfate include hypotension and prolonged bleeding time. 3. Sodium thiosulfate injection is indicated for sequential use with sodium nitrite in cases of cyanide poisoning, which may result from inhalation, ingestion, or dermal exposure to cyanide-containing compounds, including smoke from enclosed-space fires. 4. The diagnosis of cyanide poisoning is often uncertain, as there is no widely available, rapid, confirmatory blood test for cyanide. Treatment decisions must rely on clinical history and signs and symptoms of cyanide intoxication. 5. If cyanide poisoning is strongly suspected, sodium thiosulfate and sodium nitrite injections should be administered without delay. 6. In some cases, symptoms such as tachypnea, vomiting, confusion, disorientation, or mydriasis may mimic early signs of cyanide poisoning but can also occur with other toxic exposures. 7. Expert advice from a regional poison control center can be obtained by calling 1-800-222-1222. 8. Not all victims of smoke inhalation will have cyanide poisoning, as they may present with burns, trauma, or exposure to other toxic substances, complicating the diagnosis. 9. Smoke-inhalation victims should be assessed for exposure to fire or smoke in an enclosed area and the presence of soot around the mouth, nose, or oropharynx. 10. Hypotension, while suggestive of cyanide poisoning, is only present in a small percentage of cyanide-poisoned smoke inhalation victims. 11. Plasma lactate concentrations greater than or equal to 10 mmol/L may indicate cyanide poisoning but should not delay treatment. 12. Caution is advised when administering other cyanide antidotes simultaneously with sodium thiosulfate, as the safety of co-administration has not been established. If another antidote is used, it should not be administered through the same IV line. 13. Comprehensive treatment of acute cyanide intoxication requires support of vital functions, including airway management, ventilation, circulatory support, and oxygen administration, which should not be delayed for antidote administration. 14. Sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate injections are administered by slow intravenous injection, with sodium nitrite given first, followed immediately by sodium thiosulfate. Blood pressure must be monitored during infusion, and the rate of infusion should be decreased if significant hypotension occurs. 15. If signs of poisoning reappear, repeat treatment with half the original dose of both sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate. 16. In patients with known anemia, the dosage of sodium nitrite should be reduced proportionally to the hemoglobin concentration. 17. All parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration. 18. Patients should be monitored for at least 24-48 hours after sodium thiosulfate administration for adequate oxygenation, perfusion, and recurrent signs of cyanide toxicity. Hemoglobin/hematocrit levels should be obtained when treatment is initiated. 19. Standard pulse oximetry and calculated oxygen saturation values based on measured PO2 are unreliable in the presence of methemoglobinemia. 20. Chemical incompatibility has been reported between sodium thiosulfate and hydroxocobalamin; these drugs should not be administered simultaneously through the same IV line. 21. Sodium thiosulfate may contain trace impurities of sodium sulfite, but this should not deter its use in emergency situations, even in sulfite-sensitive patients. 22. Adverse reactions reported in association with sodium thiosulfate include hypotension, headache, disorientation, nausea, vomiting, prolonged bleeding time, a salty taste in the mouth, and a warm sensation over the body. Rapid administration of concentrated or improperly prepared solutions has been associated with a higher incidence of nausea and vomiting. 23. Formal drug interaction studies have not been conducted with sodium thiosulfate. 24. Sodium thiosulfate is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA, meaning it should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 25. It is not known whether sodium thiosulfate is excreted in human milk. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication to its use in life-threatening situations, but caution should be exercised. 26. Sodium thiosulfate is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and the risk of adverse reactions may be greater in patients with impaired renal function, particularly elderly patients. Renal function should be monitored, and dose selection should be cautious. 27. There is no FDA guidance on the use of sodium thiosulfate in specific gender, racial, or immunocompromised populations, or in patients with hepatic impairment. 28. Sodium thiosulfate is not systemically absorbed when taken orally. Most of it is oxidized to sulfate or incorporated into endogenous sulfur compounds, with a small proportion excreted unchanged by the kidneys. 29. The serum half-life of sodium thiosulfate after intravenous injection is approximately 20 minutes for a 1 g dose but increases significantly with higher doses. 30. Long-term animal studies have not been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenicity of sodium thiosulfate. It has not been found to be mutagenic in bacterial reverse mutation assays. 31. The efficacy of sodium thiosulfate in treating cyanide poisoning has been demonstrated primarily in animal models, with limited human data available. 32. Sodium thiosulfate should be stored at controlled room temperature (20°C to 25°C) and protected from direct light. It should not be frozen. 33. Patients should be informed of the possibility of hypotension and the need for close monitoring of blood pressure and oxygenation during treatment. 34. The interaction between alcohol and sodium thiosulfate has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while on this medication.
